title: How do you design REST error responses properly — why is returning `200 OK` with `{"success": false}` an anti-pattern (clients, monitoring, and retry logic all key off the HTTP status, so failures must use 400 bad input / 401-403 auth / 404 not found / 409 conflict / 500 server error), and what makes a good error body (a consistent shape with a STABLE machine-readable error code separate from the human-readable message, a trace/correlation id, and NO leaked stack traces — all mapped centrally through `@RestControllerAdvice` rather than per-controller `try/catch`)?
shortTitle: How do you design REST error responses properly, and why is returning 200 OK with {"success": false} an anti-pattern

s1_definition.profdef: A well-designed REST error response uses the correct HTTP status code to signal the category of failure, and carries a consistent body that includes a stable machine-readable error code separate from a human-readable message, plus a trace or correlation id for debugging, and never leaks internal stack traces. Returning 200 OK with a success false flag is an anti-pattern because clients, caches, proxies, and monitoring all key off the HTTP status, so a failure disguised as 200 is invisible to the entire ecosystem. Error mapping should be centralised with a RestControllerAdvice rather than scattered try-catch blocks in each controller.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine every rejected form at National Bank of India came back with a green approved stamp but a tiny handwritten note saying actually rejected. The filing robots, the manager's dashboard, and the auto-resubmit clerk all only look at the stamp, so they treat every rejection as a success, and the real problem stays hidden. The right way is a clearly coloured rejection stamp (the status code), a reference number for the reason (the stable error code), a plain explanation (the message), and a ticket number so support can trace it (the correlation id), with all rejection handling done at one central desk, not reinvented at every counter.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use the right status code for the failure, return a consistent body with a stable error code, a message, and a trace id, never leak stack traces, and map it all centrally with RestControllerAdvice.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A well-designed REST error response uses the correct HTTP status code to signal the category of failure, and carries a consistent body that includes a stable machine-readable error code separate from a human-readable message, plus a trace or correlation id for debugging, and never leaks internal stack traces. Returning 200 OK with a success false flag is an anti-pattern because clients, caches, proxies, and monitoring all key off the HTTP status, so a failure disguised as 200 is invisible to the entire ecosystem. Error mapping should be centralised with a RestControllerAdvice rather than scattered try-catch blocks in each controller.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine every rejected form at National Bank of India came back with a green approved stamp but a tiny handwritten note saying actually rejected. The filing robots, the manager's dashboard, and the auto-resubmit clerk all only look at the stamp, so they treat every rejection as a success, and the real problem stays hidden. The right way is a clearly coloured rejection stamp (the status code), a reference number for the reason (the stable error code), a plain explanation (the message), and a ticket number so support can trace it (the correlation id), with all rejection handling done at one central desk, not reinvented at every counter.

**One line to remember:** Use the right status code for the failure, return a consistent body with a stable error code, a message, and a trace id, never leak stack traces, and map it all centrally with RestControllerAdvice.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's old transfer API returned 200 with a body saying success false whenever a transfer failed. The operations dashboard showed everything green during an incident where thousands of transfers were failing, because it counted HTTP status, not body contents, so no alert fired and the outage ran for an hour undetected. This is exactly why failures must use real error status codes, so monitoring can see them.

Problem 2 — The mobile team wrote switch logic on the human message text, so when the bank reworded insufficient funds to balance too low for marketing reasons, the app's error handling broke overnight. This is exactly why the error body needs a stable machine code separate from the message, so clients switch on the code and the wording can change freely.

Problem 3 — During debugging, the old API returned full Java stack traces in the response, exposing class names and even a database error, which both leaked internals and confused the app. This is why a good error body carries a trace id that links to server logs instead of dumping the stack trace to the client.

We will build a transfer service with a RestControllerAdvice that maps each exception to the correct status and a consistent ApiError body carrying a stable code, a message, and a trace id, with no stack traces. The demo triggers an insufficient funds failure, a not found failure, and an unexpected failure, showing proper codes and bodies.

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/error-handling-service-1.0.0.jar

# 422 INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS (stable code + message + traceId)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"CUR3001","to":"SAV2001","amount":9999999}'
# {"code":"INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS","message":"Balance is too low...","traceId":"...","timestamp":"..."}

# 404 ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV9999","to":"SAV2001","amount":100}'

# 500 INTERNAL_ERROR — generic message, NO stack trace leaked (trace is in logs)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CRASH","amount":100}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three POSTs — a transfer exceeding Priya's balance, a transfer from a non-existent account, and a transfer that triggers an unexpected failure.

Step 1: The over-balance transfer reaches the controller, which has no try-catch, so it calls the service. The service throws InsufficientFundsException. The exception bubbles up to the central RestControllerAdvice.

Step 2: The advice matches InsufficientFundsException, generates a trace id, logs the full stack trace keyed by that trace id, and returns 422 Unprocessable Entity with an ApiError body carrying the stable code INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, the human message, the trace id, and a timestamp. The client switches on the code, not the message.

Step 3: The missing-account transfer throws AccountNotFoundException, which the advice maps to 404 with code ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND and a fresh trace id. The shape is identical to step 2, so the client parses it with the same code.

Step 4: The crash transfer throws a generic RuntimeException. The catch-all handler maps it to 500 with code INTERNAL_ERROR and a generic message, while the full stack trace goes only to the logs under the trace id. The client sees no internal details, and support can find the exact log by the trace id the customer reports.

Step 5: In every case the HTTP status is correct, so monitoring counts the 422 and 404 as client issues and the 500 as a server error, and retry logic can act appropriately. Nothing is disguised as 200.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 22:15:00 WARN  POST /transfers over-balance -> 422
{"code":"INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS","message":"Balance is too low for this transfer","traceId":"a1b2c3","timestamp":"2026-10-25T22:15:00Z"}
2026-10-25 22:15:01 WARN  POST /transfers SAV9999 -> 404
{"code":"ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND","message":"One of the accounts does not exist","traceId":"d4e5f6","timestamp":"..."}
2026-10-25 22:15:02 ERROR traceId=g7h8i9 code=INTERNAL_ERROR status=500 (full stack trace in log only)
{"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"An unexpected error occurred","traceId":"g7h8i9","timestamp":"..."}
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Error Response Design ═══

  ┌─ Rules ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  status reflects category: 400/401/403/404/409/422/500  │
  │  body = ApiError{code, message, traceId, timestamp}     │
  │  code STABLE (contract) ; message free to change        │
  │  NO stack trace in body → logs only, keyed by traceId   │
  │  central @RestControllerAdvice, not per-controller try  │
  │  NEVER 200 with success:false                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │     TransferController        │  no try/catch
  │  + create(req): 201 / throws  │
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ throws
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   GlobalExceptionHandler      │  @RestControllerAdvice
  │  + notFound → 404             │
  │  + funds → 422                │
  │  + unexpected → 500           │
  │  - build(status,code,msg,e)   │  log trace, build ApiError
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (insufficient funds) ──────────
  1. POST /transfers over balance
  2.   → service.transfer → throw InsufficientFundsException
  3.   → advice.funds → traceId=UUID, log.error(traceId, e)
  4.   → 422 + ApiError{INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, msg, traceId}
  Contract: every error = same shape, correct status, no leak
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A REST error response is designed around two things: the correct HTTP status code and a consistent, safe error body. The status code signals the category of failure, so bad input is 400, authentication is 401, permission is 403, missing is 404, conflict is 409, a business-rule failure on valid input is 422, and an unexpected server failure is 500. This matters because the status is the one field that clients, caches, proxies, and monitoring all read, so it must be honest.

That is exactly why returning 200 OK with a success false flag is an anti-pattern. At National Bank of India our old transfer API did this, and during a real incident where thousands of transfers were failing, the operations dashboard stayed completely green, because it counts HTTP status and not body contents, so no alert fired and the outage ran undetected for an hour. On top of that, clients treat 2xx as success and never trigger their error paths, and retry logic never retries a 200 even if the real failure was a transient server error. Disguising a failure as 200 defeats the entire purpose of HTTP.

A good error body is consistent across every endpoint and separates a stable machine-readable code from a human-readable message. The code, like INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, is part of the API contract and never changes, so client logic switches on it reliably, while the message can be reworded or localised freely. We learned this the hard way when the mobile team switched on the message text and a marketing rewording broke the app overnight. The body also carries a trace id that appears in the server logs so support can find the exact request, and it never includes a stack trace, because that leaks internals and helps attackers; stack traces go to the logs under the trace id.

Finally, all of this is mapped in one place using a RestControllerAdvice, not scattered try-catch blocks in every controller. Centralising it guarantees that every endpoint returns the same shape, the same status rules, and the same safe behaviour, so the controllers stay clean and just let exceptions bubble up. That combination — correct status, stable code separate from message, a trace id, no stack traces, and central mapping — is what makes a banking API's errors both debuggable for us and reliable for every client and monitoring tool that depends on them.
